## A1: Give the net the evidence it can't see: an oracle-ceiling test first, then speed/damage evidence and action history as inputs
- lever: network/architecture (inputs)
- generations: both
- mechanism: Measured fact: the opponent-set posterior in the v2 observation is filtered by revealed constraints only. The encoder says so: "v2.0 uses no speed / damage evidence" (`src/porygon/v2/encoder.py:9`, `consistent_revealed` at :122). The spec also has no history: no last action, no move order, no damage dealt (`src/porygon/v2/spec.py` MON_NUM / FIELD_NUM). So the net can't tell that the opponent outsped it last turn (Scarf, Unburden, boosted Speed), that a hit was bigger than any unboosted set allows (Band/Specs), or that the opponent clicked the same move twice (a choice lock). Our search's world sampler uses exactly this evidence (methods §5.2). So does Foul Play ("Set prediction is as important as, if not more important than, accurate and fast search", https://pmariglia.github.io/posts/foul-play/). Jaxcalibur has 16 history tokens and keeps its set predictions across turns (https://jaxcalibur.github.io/). I infer this is a structural cause of the short-game deficit. KO races turn on speed order and damage thresholds. The P8 pattern ("set up at < 50% HP while slower") is defined on true speed, which the net cannot observe. Self-play hides the problem because both sides are equally blind (flat by length in self-play, loss-patterns §1). More training cannot supply a missing input.
  - Change, spec v2.2: (a) filter the posterior by speed order and per-hit damage range, porting `porygon.inference`'s checks to the Python and JS encoders; (b) add per-mon history scalars: moved first last turn, last move, count of consecutive uses of the same move, and the last hit's damage as a fraction of the predicted range.
  - The new input columns start at zero (Net2Net, arXiv 1511.05641), so the branch starts as exactly the old net.
- evidence for: oracle ceilings for our gen4 search: true sets of revealed mons +2.9 ± 3.9, whole team +5.2 ± 3.7 (fp4-07/08). With the older, weaker inference the same oracle was worth +8.8 (fp4-10); I infer that information is worth more the blinder the player is. Short-game gap 53.4 vs 64.6 (dg-08). Plus the Jaxcalibur and Foul Play designs above.
- evidence against / prior attempts: not in the tried list. bc-15/g9q-28 changed data and bn-01 changed capacity, not inputs. dg-05 ("inference near ceiling") is about the search's sampler, which already has the evidence; the net doesn't. Weak evidence against: no team feature, Choice items included, explained the length gap (loss-patterns §1).
- predicted effect: +1.5 [0, +3] vs FP @200k. I guess a net oracle ceiling of ≈ +3 by analogy with fp4-07, and that evidence features recover 30–60% of it, plus an unknown amount from history.
- cost:
  - Kill test: ≈ 1 engineering day (an oracle flag in the JS encoder that copies the aux targets, which already hold the true set, into the observation) and ≈ 1 CPU-h on the data host or VM.
  - Scale-up: 4–6 engineering days (port + parity fixtures), then 100–200M A40 steps (1.5–3 days).
  - Risk to the main run: none, G9q is untouched.
- kill test: in-process spd_h2h, cd@2030 at T 0.5 on both sides, 5000 duplicate pairs per arm.
  - Arm O: our side sees the oracle (true item, ability, tera, moves and exact stats) for revealed opponent mons.
  - Arm Oₛ: only the true item and true Speed, about what evidence can recover.
  - Both arms play unmodified cd@2030.
  - Pre-registered rule: KILL if O < 52.0 (if a perfect oracle is worth < 2 points, partial evidence is worth < 1). GO if Oₛ's lower 95% bound > 50.5. Report by game length.
- scale-up if GO: implement v2.2 and branch G9-EV from the latest G9q checkpoint on the A40. Pre-register cooled vs cooled against G9q at matched steps (sequential, θ₁ 52%). Then 1000 games vs FP @200k and vs pure search. Fold into the next new main lineage.
- failure modes / confounds:
  - Oracle inputs are off-distribution early in the game (everything known at turn 1), which could bias the ceiling either way.
  - A self-play ceiling may understate the value against searchers, which punish misreads.
  - Bugs in the parity between the JS and Python encoders.
- formal check: if the new input weights W_e = 0, then f_θ′(x, e) = f_θ(x) for every e. This is trivial; a unit test is enough.

## A2: Purify the deployed policy (play cooler than T 0.5)
- lever: other (test-time policy)
- generations: both
- mechanism: Fact: raw nets, and lookahead2's a_net, sample at T 0.5 (methods §6.4; `lookahead2.py` docstring step 1). That setting comes from v1 (v1-19, T 0.5 vs T 1 +2.3; "cooler gained nothing for v1", methods §6.4) and was never tested on v2. v2 trains with entropy 0.01, a zero-avoid term 0.003 and an entropy floor of 0.35 in cooldowns (methods §4.2/4.3). All three put mass on non-best actions on purpose, to keep exploring. Against opponents that don't adapt to our mixing within a game, purification or thresholding of a mixed strategy beats playing it as is (Ganzfried, Sandholm & Waugh, AAMAS 2012, https://ifaamas.org/Proceedings/aamas2012/papers/3E_4.pdf; Obscuro: full system 70.2% vs its no-purification variant, literature report §5). Memoryless nets and Foul Play's per-decision search don't adapt in that way (I infer). In KO races a single off-policy sample loses the game, which fits the short-game deficit (dg-08).
  - Arms: T 0.25; T 0.1 (≈ argmax); thresholding (drop actions with p < 0.1, then T 0.5).
- evidence for: v1-19 (cooling from T 1 already paid +2.3 once); the purification literature above.
- evidence against / prior attempts: §6.4 / v1-19 are v1-only, so they don't cover a v2 policy trained with zero-avoid and an entropy floor. Jaxcalibur's author names "a tendency to become predictable" as a weakness (jaxcalibur.github.io): purity can be exploited by adaptive humans.
- predicted effect: +0.5 [−1, +2] vs FP @200k. My guess is that T 0.5 already removes most low-probability mass, so the gain comes from the near-split decisions.
- cost: half a day of engineering (a temperature or threshold flag on the player); ≈ 1 CPU-h in-process; one 1000-game FP run (≈ 2 h on the slot). No risk to the main run.
- kill test: in-process spd_h2h, cd@2030 at T′ vs cd@2030 at T 0.5, 5000 pairs per arm. KILL all arms if none has a lower 95% bound > 50.0. Otherwise, run only the best arm vs FP @200k with seed 8203222. That replays g9q-32's team pairs, so the difference is paired. Adopt if the paired difference is > 0 and its lower 95% bound is > −1.5. The headline is then re-measured with a new seed.
- scale-up if GO: apply the same purification to lookahead2's a_net, re-derive δ with the precision rule (ns-13/15 method), and run an LA2 adoption test.
- failure modes / confounds: the in-process opponent is the same memoryless net, so it can't exploit predictability; the gain may not hold against humans. Check on a challenge/ladder sample before the thesis claims it.
- formal check: none

## A3: Tactical sparring partners in the PPO league
- lever: opponent/league
- generations: gen9 first
- mechanism: Fact: the training opponents are 49% self, 36% frozen nets, 10% snapshots and 5% heuristic / max-power baselines (BRIEF; `train.py:1375`). None of them calculates. The short-game deficit shows up only against search: flat in self-play, reversed against BC (loss-patterns §1; dg-01/07/08). An exploiter that is itself a net finds nothing (ns-30). I infer that it shares the learner's blind spots, while a calculating opponent plays lines PPO never has to defend against. League diversity and exploiters were needed for robustness in AlphaStar (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1724-z).
  - Change: p_search = 5–10% of pool battles against our own pure gen9 search (`search.py`: poke-engine MCTS, our inference). The budget is small, or a single true-state world to save cost.
  - Hard rules: no Foul Play code, and nothing models Foul Play. The gate is measured against our own search, lookahead2 and nets.
  - **Flag for the orchestrator:** poke-engine and Foul Play have the same author and the same engine family. Please rule explicitly on whether this counts as general strength.
- evidence for: loss-patterns §1, dg-08, ns-30. Our search is a different but beatable opponent (g9q-23: raw net 55.5% against it).
- evidence against / prior attempts: bc-12…14, v1-12 and ns-27/28 used search as a *teacher* to imitate. Here it is only an *opponent*, and learning stays PPO on win/loss. The "no search in training" lessons from MissingNo.Zero and Jaxcalibur (literature report §8) are about search inside the learner.
- predicted effect: +1.5 [0, +3.5] vs FP. Upper bound: closing the cd@2030 short-game gap is worth ≈ 0.35 × 11.2 ≈ 3.9 points. The ≈ 35% short-game share is derived from dg-08's interval width.
- cost:
  - Engineering: 4–6 days (feed the fastenv protocol stream into a Python poke-env Battle, then `search.convert`, then the engine, inside a pool worker).
  - CPU: ≈ 1–2 CPUs at 5% of battles and ≈ 20 ms per search decision.
  - GPU and slot: 2 × 35M A40 steps (≈ 13 h) and 2 slot runs of ≈ 2 h.
  - Risk to G9q: none.
- kill test:
  - **Step 0 (free; rule fixed before reading):** split the existing games of g9q-23 and g9q-16 (raw net vs pure search) by length, if their results log turns as fp9's do (dg-07). KILL if short (< 25 turns) minus long is > −4 points: our search doesn't reproduce the weakness, so it is the wrong sparring partner.
  - **Step 1:** two arms from the latest G9q checkpoint, each 30M steps plus a 5M cooldown: control (today's mix) and S (10% of pool battles against search). Both play pure search on the netv2 vs-search harness, same seed, 1000 games each (paired). Then S vs control in-process, 2000 pairs.
  - GO if S − control vs search is ≥ +3.0 with a lower 95% bound > 0, AND S vs control in-process has a lower 95% bound > 48.5.
- scale-up if GO: run the search opponent in the next main lineage. Measure vs FP @200k, lookahead2 and the length split.
- failure modes / confounds: 30M steps may be too few to learn the change; the net may overfit to our search's quirks (check against lookahead2); the slower opponent shifts the batch composition; harness offset (cal-03), so both arms use one harness.
- formal check: none

## A4: lookahead2 against the predicted opponent, not the worst-case one
- lever: search
- generations: gen9
- mechanism: Fact: lookahead2 scores Q(a) against the RM+ equilibrium of a zero-sum Bayesian game in which the opponent knows the world, and forced switch-ins take the one worst for us (`lookahead2.py` docstring, steps 3–4). I infer that this estimate is conservative. In KO races the equilibrium opponent always has the punishing reply, so a_L rarely clears δ, and the gain disappears in short games (la2-len1: short −3.0 ± 7.7). Real opponents are not equilibrium players. Our net's opponent-action head is trained on opponents' policies (spec `aux_opp_target`), and Jaxcalibur mixes such a prior into its search (jaxcalibur.github.io).
  - Change: y_k^λ = (1−λ)·y_k^RM + λ·q_k, where q_k is the head restricted to world k's options (`deepen.opp_prior` / `opp_classes` already do the mapping).
  - Then Q_λ(a) = Σₖ wₖ Mₖ[a]·y_k^λ and a_L = argmax Q_λ. λ = 0 is today's bot.
  - This is KL-regularised search toward a behaviour model (piKL, https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.07544). Keeping a minimax component is the safe-exploitation idea (Ganzfried & Sandholm, https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2716322).
  - The head models generic competent play and is never trained on Foul Play.
- evidence for: Jaxcalibur's design above; la2-len1; ns-20 (LA2's total gain is small, +1.3).
- evidence against / prior attempts:
  - fpr-307072/307076 changed the root solver (root_game, rm_gamma), not the opponent model.
  - deepen used q only for expansion priority (methods §5.6), and ns-25 tested budget, not the opponent model.
  - Risk: the head predicts our own net, so it may mispredict other bots.
- predicted effect: +1 [−0.5, +2.5] vs FP. This assumes about half of LA2's lost short-game value is recovered.
- cost: 1 engineering day; offline δ calibration in CPU-minutes; ≈ 12 h of slot time.
- kill test:
  - First, pick δ_λ for λ = 0.5 offline so that it matches the benchmark's override rate on the 1,403-position study set. This separates "which moves change" from "how many".
  - Then LA2-λ0.5 vs the LA2 benchmark (cd@2030, δ 0.0025) on the Showdown fastenv slot, sequential 50 → 54% (the Bet 1 design, ns-14), n_max 600 pairs. KILL at futility; GO if the MUE lower bound is > 50.
- scale-up if GO: run λ ∈ {0.25, 0.75} as parallel arms, then a fixed-n FP @200k headline.
- failure modes / confounds: errors in the head-to-option mapping in some worlds; a miscalibrated head for unfamiliar opponents; matching override rates may still change which positions get overridden.
- formal check: for fixed matrices Mₖ, Q_λ is affine in λ, so Q_λ(a) ≥ Q₀(a) − λ·max_k |Mₖ[a]·(q_k − y_k)|. This bounds the worst-case loss against an equilibrium opponent by λ times the head's deviation. It is provable directly from linearity.

## A5: gen4 — move the gen4 bot onto the v2 net plus lookahead2
- lever: search
- generations: gen4
- mechanism: Fact: the gen4 headline is still search + fitted eval + the v1 prior (fp4-04, 59.2, time-based). The R1b-F net didn't help as a prior *inside* MCTS (v2g4-11/12, inconclusive). R1b-F raw @300M scored 55.6 (v2g4-10, 400 games) and kept improving: @552.7M beat @300M 55.2% (v2g4-15). In gen9 the net-first stack overtook search (g9q-23, ns-24).
  - Change: cool R1b-F's latest checkpoint (≈ 630M), port lookahead2 to gen4 (gen4 LeafEncoder and engine build; `search.convert` is already generation-parametric), and re-baseline both gen4 bots against FP @200k.
  - This also lets A1, A2 and A4 carry over to gen4.
- evidence for: v2g4-15; the gen9 path ns-14/24.
- evidence against / prior attempts: v2g4-11/12 put the net inside MCTS as a prior; here the net plays and search only gates it.
- predicted effect: raw R1b-F-cd ≈ 57–59 vs FP. I infer this from +5.2 h2h by 552M and the ≈ 0.5 h2h-to-FP transfer seen in gen9 (g9q-21…32). LA2 adds +1, giving 58–60: parity with fp4-04 at worst.
- cost: 2–3 engineering days; a 5M-step cooldown on the T4 (≈ 3.5 h at 400 sps) without stopping R1b-F; ≈ 8 h of slot time.
- kill test: raw R1b-F-cd vs FP gen4 @200k, 1000 games (≈ 2 h). Pre-registered: stop the gen4 net route for now if the point estimate is < 55.0. GO to LA2-gen4 vs the same raw net, sequential 50 → 54%.
- scale-up if GO: LA2-gen4 vs the gen4 search bot at 200k (1000 games); adopt if it is non-inferior with a 3-point margin.
- failure modes / confounds: fp4-04 is time-based, so compare only within the re-baselined 200k runs; the gen4 LeafEncoder needs parity checks; T4 contention.
- formal check: none

MEMBER A TOP PICK: A1 — the net cannot see speed order, damage rolls or move history, which plausibly drives the short-game deficit and which no amount of training can fix, and about one engineering day plus one CPU-hour of oracle h2h settles whether the lever is worth ≥ 2 points.
